opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, it's because the day-to-day work tends to pull you into a very narrow frame. When you're deep in it, you're thinking about the next grant decision, the next report, whether some benchmark result holds up, how to phrase a particular argument. Each of those things matters, but it's easy to spend weeks at that zoom level and lose the thread of why any of it matters.

And the stakes of the bigger picture keep rising. If you take seriously that we might be a few years away from AI systems that can do most of what humans do, maybe including AI research itself, that's an enormous claim. It should be shaping how I prioritize, what I'm willing to let slide, which conversations I think are urgent. But the immediate pressures of work don't automatically keep that in view. Ironically, the busier and more consequential the work gets, the easier it is to treat it as a to-do list rather than as a response to something genuinely world-changing.

So I've come to think I need something deliberately separate, whether that's reading broadly, long walks thinking about where this is all going, or conversations with people outside my immediate circle, where the point isn't to produce anything. It's to step back and ask: given everything I believe about how this technology might unfold, am I actually working on the right things? Am I still updating? What would I be embarrassed to have missed in two years?

There's also an emotional piece. This field can be grinding and anxious, and reconnecting with the larger picture, both the risks and the really hopeful possibilities, is part of what keeps the work meaningful rather than just stressful. Without that, I think you burn out, or you drift into optimizing for things that are locally legible but not what actually matters.

r001.rationale: She says immediate work pressures do not automatically keep the bigger picture in view, making it easy to lose sight of why the work matters.

r002.rationale: She describes how busy, grinding work narrows her focus and says she needs a separate practice to step back and reconnect with the larger picture.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that the day-to-day of this work has a way of shrinking your field of view without you noticing. When I'm deep in a grant evaluation, or going back and forth on some forecasting question about compute trends or when a particular capability shows up, I'm operating on a very local objective function. Is this argument right? Is this number plausible? Did this org do what they said they'd do? Those are real questions and they deserve care, but they're all one or two steps removed from the thing I actually care about, which is something like: does the transition to a world with very capable AI go well for people?

And the trouble is that the local questions are also the ones that give you feedback. You can finish a memo. You can resolve a disagreement. The bigger picture doesn't give you that. There's no moment where you check the box on "humanity is handling this okay." So if you're not deliberate about it, your attention just drifts toward whatever has a satisfying loop, and over months you can find that you've been very productive and also kind of lost the thread of why any of it matters.

The other thing is that my views on the big picture have actually changed a lot, and I think they changed partly because I forced myself to step back. The timelines work is a good example. The whole point of that was to sit with the question of what the world looks like if this goes faster than people expect, and that's not a thing you arrive at by iterating on the next grant. If I'd only been doing the incremental stuff, I think I would have just been slowly updating at the margin and never actually confronting how different my picture had become.

So the practice, to the extent I have one, is partly about emotional honesty, just letting myself feel the weight of what I think is coming rather than treating it as an abstraction I manage professionally. And partly it's epistemic hygiene. Periodically asking: if I zoom all the way out, does the portfolio of things I'm spending my time on still look like the right bet? Because the answer has sometimes been no, and I'd rather find that out on purpose than by accident.

r001.rationale: She says day-to-day work narrows her focus and can make her lose the thread of why it matters, so it does not automatically keep her connected to her broader aspiration.

r002.rationale: She explains that local, feedback-rich work can crowd out the bigger picture, motivating a deliberate practice of stepping back and reassessing whether her work serves it.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s easy for my attention to narrow to whatever is immediately in front of me: the next decision, the next piece of work, the thing I’m worried I’m getting wrong. And even if that work is motivated by something much bigger, doing the work doesn’t necessarily keep me emotionally connected to that motivation.

So I increasingly want a separate practice of stepping back and remembering: there are all these people whose lives matter, and the future could be extraordinary, and the reason to work on these problems is to help make that possible. I don’t want that to just be an argument I endorse intellectually. I want it to feel real to me.

And I think that can change the quality of the work, too. There’s a difference between acting from a sense of care and possibility and acting because you feel like you’re perpetually behind on an urgent assignment.

r001.rationale: She says doing the work does not necessarily keep her emotionally connected to its bigger motivation.

r002.rationale: She describes attention narrowing to immediate work and worries, then says this is why she increasingly wants a separate practice to step back and reconnect with the larger purpose.

sol-6.1.text:
I think my day-to-day work can pull me into a pretty narrow frame: What’s the next thing I need to figure out? What’s the argument here? What should we do about this particular problem? And those questions matter, but I can spend a lot of time on them without really feeling connected to why I care in the first place.

So I increasingly want a separate practice where I step back and remember that this is about actual people and their lives, and about a future that could be really wonderful. Understanding intellectually that the stakes are high isn’t quite the same as having that understanding feel present. I want more room for that—for caring about the bigger picture without immediately turning it into another task.

r001.rationale: She says day-to-day work can keep her focused on narrow questions without feeling connected to why she cares.

r002.rationale: She says that this pull of daily work makes her increasingly want a separate practice to step back and reconnect with people, their lives, and the broader future.
